question.leadin: This place was originally known as the Flavian Amphitheatre.
question.text: Name this structure which included 80 entrances. Its construction began under the emperor Vespasian [veh-SPAY-zhun] and was completed under the emperor Titus.
question.clue: While not for getting sick, this location's vomitorium allowed for the rapid entrance and exits of spectators to various parts of it.

swap.text: This battle was a disastrous defeat of Hannibal by the Roman general Scipio Africanus. This battle was so detrimental to Carthage that it resulted in the immediate end of the Second Punic War.
swap.clue: The right wing of this battle was composed of cavalry under the direction of Massinissa.

question.leadin: The Batavian Revolt began during this time period, which started with an assassination led by prefect Nymphidius Sabinus.
question.text: Identify this time period which saw the rule of men like Otho and Vitelleus.
question.answerHtml: Year of the Four Emperors [prompt on “69 AD”]
question.clue: It saw the exile of Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes, after a revolt by her husband Venutius, as well as two major battles at Bedriacum or Cremona.

swap.text: This man succeeded Augustus as emperor and had earlier conquered Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Germania. As emperor, he withdrew to Capri allowing his advisor Sejanus to rule.
swap.clue: He was killed the captain of his Praetorian guard, Macro, whom he had earlier enlisted in smuggling a letter to the Senate detailing the depradation of Macro's predecessor.

question.text: This man commanded the cavalry at the Battle of Alesia. Later, this man was a member of the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Marcus Lepidus before commmitting suicide after the Battle of Actium.
question.clue: This general commanded the left wing at Pharsalus (far-SAY-lus).

swap.text: During his consulship, Cicero had to deal with a conspiracy led by this man, but Cicero was later be exiled for putting this man to death without a trial.
swap.clue: Some of his allies were executed after envoys handed over signed documents detailing their plans.

question.leadin: This woman's revolt occurred after the death of her husband Prasutagus and the rape of her two daughters.
question.text: Name this Iceni queen who revolted against the Roman Empire. She either died from sickness or via suicide after the failure of the revolt.
question.clue: This ruler trounced the Ninth Legion but was defeated by Suetonius at the Battle of Watling Street.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the lavish retirement of Lucius Licinius Lucullus.
swap.text: According to Plutarch, Pompey and this Roman statesman once tried to figure out what Lucullus ate when he was alone only to discover that he consumed a meal worth 50,000 drachmae. This statesman wrote speeches such as Pro Archia, which defended Lucullus' friend Archias, and the Philippics.
swap.clue: This man asked an opponent when he would "cease abusing our patience" at the beginning of one speech.

question.leadin: Identify these other kings of Rome.
question.text: After his son raped the noblewoman Lucretia, this last king of Rome was driven out in 509 BC by a mob led by Junius Brutus and was forced into exile in Etruria.
question.answer: Tarquinius Superbus or Tarquin the Proud
question.clue: This Roman king overthrew Servius Tullius and was himself deposed after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, leading her kinsmen to rebel.

swap.leadin: As part of the Second Triumvirate, Lepidus received this office.
swap.text: Name this chief priest of the Roman religion.
swap.clue: Per the Lex Ogulnia, the plebeian Coruncanius held this position that Marcus Aurelius held instead of Lucius Verus.

question.leadin: Tarquin the Proud, the last king of Rome, was said to have been descended from this civilization.
question.text: Name this ancient civilization, whose city of Veii ("VAY-ee") was located just north of Rome. Veii was the centre of this civilization's namesake league, which was made up of twelve cities.
question.clue: Priests of these people were the first to be called haruspices ("huh-RUSS-puh-sees") and made divinations from sheep entrails.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about recipients of the Grass Crown, the highest and rarest military honor in ancient Rome.
swap.text: Quintus Sertorius was awarded the Grass Crown for putting down a rebellion in this region, where he would later launch his own rebellion. Emperor Theodosius the Great was born in this region.
swap.answerHtml: Hispania [accept Spain, Portugal, or anything referring to the Iberian peninsula]
swap.clue: Galba and Otho simultaneously governed the two halves of this province, which was divided into Ulterior and Tarraconensis regions after the Second Punic War.

question.leadin: A 2025 book by Tom Schmidt contends that this author's namesake Testimonium was entirely genuine, rather than containing a Christian interpolation.
question.text: Name this Jewish historian who briefly discussed Jesus, John the Baptist, and James the Just in his Antiquities of the Jews.
question.answerHtml: Flavius Josephus [or Yosef ben Mattityahu; or Yoseph bar Mattityahu] (The book is Josephus and Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ.)
question.clue: That mass suicide followed this man's defeat in the siege of Jotapata.

swap.leadin: This series of conflicts occurred between 343 to 290 BCE.
swap.text: Name this series of three wars between the Roman Republic and the namesake tribe in the Apennines.
swap.clue: The Roman armies were slaughtered at Lautulae and Caudine Forks during this series of three wars in the fourth-century B.C. These wars prompted construction of the Appian Way to secure Campania.

question.leadin: Suetonius records how a ruler of this region, Ptolemy, was executed by Caligula because his purple cloak drew the attention of the crowd when he entered a theatre.
question.text: Name this region that, after its annexation by Claudius, was divided into the provinces of Tingitana and Caesariensis. Another king of this region, Bocchus I, betrayed his son-in-law, Jugurtha, to Sulla.
question.answerHtml: Mauretania [accept Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis; prompt on North Africa, Maghreb, Algeria, Morocco, or the Atlas Mountains by asking “what was the Roman name of the region?”]
question.clue: It's not Egypt, but a man named Ptolemy was the last Roman client king of this region; its earlier client kings included the Numidian prince Juba II.

swap.leadin: In a poem describing God, he wrote that God "is indescribable" even to Jesus.
swap.text: Name this author of "Thalia" whose views were criticized by Athanasius (ath-uh-NAY-shus) in On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia (uh-RIM-in-um and si-LOO-shuh)
swap.clue: While speaking at an event, this person was apocryphally slapped by an outraged man from Patara.

question.text: When Rome first conquered Lusitania, there was an anti-Roman rebellion led by this man. Livy started the tradition that this man was a shepherd, which is how he is portrayed in the Lusiads.
question.clue: This former shepherd and leader of the Lusitani rose up against Roman control after a governor dug a trench around a group of Lusitani and killed them while they were surrendering their weapons. This leader defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Mt. Veneris.

swap.leadin: This man lost an eye while serving in Gaul as a quaestor responsible for recruiting troops for the Social War.
swap.text: Name this Roman general who went rogue in the 70s CE and assumed personal rule of several western Roman provinces before Quintus Metellus and Pompey marched against him, inspiring his confederate Vento to assassinate him.
swap.clue: Along with his lieutenant Hirtuleius, he overthrew the governor Quintus Metellus Pius, and then was joined by Marcus Perpenna, though Perpenna eventually had this man murdered at a banquet.

question.leadin: Identify the following about monumental columns.
question.text: Mainz was home to a classical column dedicated in honor of Nero to this aspect of the chief god of the Roman state, whose official worship took place at his temple on the Capitoline. The Mainz column was a model for other columns erected to worship this god elsewhere in northern Europe.

swap.text: The First Punic War was sparked by this group of Italian mercenaries, who requested Carthaginian aid after losing to Hieron II, but switched to the Roman side when the Carthaginian army arrived.
swap.clue: Pyrrhus was also opposed by this band of mercenaries hired by Agathocles, the Tyrant of Syracuse. They later sided with Rome against Syracuse and Carthage during the First Punic War.
